articles.title: Wu Shicun on why Beijing will not rule out Scarborough Shoal construction
articles.summary:
- **Philippines' "assertive transparency" strategy**: Wu describes Manila's approach as deliberately provoking confrontations at Renai Jiao (Second Thomas Shoal) since 2023, then packaging viral videos to portray China as a bully and the Philippines as a victim, partly to secure more budget and equipment for its coast guard.

- **China's diplomatic focus on rule-making**: Beijing concentrates its diplomatic capital on institutional frameworks, including over a decade of Code of Conduct (COC) negotiations since 2013 and the 56th session of working group meetings on the Declaration on Conduct of Parties (DOC), held in Vietnam.

- **China's narrative shift**: Wu acknowledges that China was initially caught off-guard by the Philippines' public relations tactics and Western media support but has since adjusted, proactively countering Manila's false narratives and proposing to construct a new South China Sea narrative.

- **Broader strategic adjustment**: Wu frames China's evolving communications approach as a "profound paradigm shift" expected to become more proactive, positioning China as a responsible major power committed to telling the truth.

articles.title: Susan Thornton on US-China ties, post-midterms and averting a new balloon crisis
articles.summary:
- Susan Thornton, a former acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, described the Trump-Xi summit as "necessary" and the only effective guardrail in US-China relations, noting that Trump has now held two summits with Xi and calling for regularisation of such high-level meetings.

- She argued that US-China summits are always held to a higher bar with long lists of expected outcomes, making them difficult to organise, and suggested that normalising these meetings—without requiring extensive deliverables each time—is essential to keeping the relationship on track.

- On avoiding disruptive incidents like the 2023 balloon crisis or Pelosi's 2022 Taiwan visit, Thornton framed the issue as achieving "constructive strategic stability" by identifying and managing issues that could escalate into worst-case scenarios or conflict.

- She noted that progress has been made under the current administration on recognising these risk factors, and that Trump appears to have reflected on the deterioration of US-China relations during his first term (2017–2021), particularly around Covid-19.

articles.title: Zheng Yongnian on Trump, Venezuela and why China doesn’t want ‘a separate kitchen’
articles.summary:
• **Zheng Yongnian describes Trump's strategic shift as a move from the Monroe Doctrine to the "Donroe Doctrine"** — consolidating US influence in the western hemisphere and practicing "offshore balancing" by retreating from global commitments in Europe, the Middle East, and East Asia, with broad consensus in the US as reflected in the latest National Security Strategy.

• **The US pivot to Latin America will cause significant disruption**, just as withdrawal from other regions will create local chaos; Zheng predicts "turbulence" as the defining trend of coming years, with major adjustments unfolding whether the US retreats or advances.

• **Changes are occurring at three levels**: big-power relations (where major geopolitical shifts are driven), the rise of assertive "regional lords" such as Turkey, and disruption to smaller states caught in between.

• **Zheng notes that Venezuela is unlikely to be the US's last target**, and that discussions within American right-wing think tanks about a "tripartite partition of the world" mirror similar ambitions long pursued by Russian President Vladimir Putin — a dynamic that alarms European nations like Poland, who fear Ukraine will not be Russia's final objective.

• **China's response**, per Zheng's framing, involves navigating this shifting order without seeking to create a separate sphere of influence, though the full details of China's stance are not completed in the provided excerpt.

articles.title: Liu Qian on Chinese innovation, the US rivalry and women holding up half the sky
articles.summary:
• The US-China rivalry has expanded beyond trade into technology, ideologies, and global collaboration, and Liu Qian warns that continued unhealthy competition will harm both countries and the world.

• Concerns about US tariff impacts on China's economy are exaggerated: exports to the US made up only about 2.8% of China's GDP last year (exports overall were ~19% of GDP, with US-bound exports comprising 14.7% of that total). ASEAN and the EU are now larger export markets than the US.

• China's export portfolio has diversified significantly: China's largest export destination is now ASEAN, exports to Brazil grew 23.3% last year, and exports to Africa grew 25.9% in the first eight months of this year. Exports to the US have declined from a peak where total exports comprised 36% of GDP to the current 19%.

• While broader risks remain — including unemployment, weakened private consumption, clouded business sentiment, and supply chain disruptions — Chinese exporters have demonstrated resilience and creativity, adapting through new markets, products, and routes, with exports generally holding steady.

• Liu Qian is the founder of Wusawa Advisory, formerly managing director of The Economist Group in Greater China, and the only Chinese representative in the core working group of the UN Women Leaders Network, advocating for gender equality in policymaking.

articles.title: Fuchsia Dunlop tells how she fell for China’s cuisine and names her perfect dish
articles.summary:
- **Fuchsia Dunlop** is a British author and chef widely regarded as the Western world's foremost expert on Chinese cuisine, particularly Sichuanese food, having written seven popular books on the subject.

- She first went to China in **1994** as a British Council postgraduate student at Sichuan University in Chengdu, where she began learning to cook by studying in local restaurant kitchens and attending the **Sichuan Higher Institute of Cuisine**.

- After a three-month chef's training course with **50 young Sichuan chefs**, she returned to England and discovered a notable absence of English-language Sichuan cookbooks, motivating her to write the first one, published in **2001**.

- Her passion for regional Chinese food diversity is evident in her preference for lesser-known **mooncake varieties** — savoury minced pork mooncakes from Shanghai and Yunnan-style mooncakes with Yunnan ham or rose petal jam — over the more commonly known Cantonese lotus seed paste versions.

- She describes Chinese cuisine as an endlessly rewarding subject due to the country's vast size and regional diversity, noting that **Sichuan food has since become highly popular** in Britain, a stark contrast to when she began her research.

articles.title: Robin Xing on how China’s ‘two-speed’ economy can solve contrasting problems
articles.summary:
• **China's "K-shaped" economy**: Robin Xing, chief China economist at Morgan Stanley, sees a divergence in China's economy, with the "top half of the K" — driven by an estimated US$6 trillion in factory upgrade investments in robotics, smart machinery, industrial software, and power grids — potentially offsetting deflation and weak consumption.

• **US-China trade trajectory**: Xing expects Xi-Trump meetings to steer bilateral ties toward "managed competition," with modestly expanded cooperation in non-sensitive sectors (trade, agriculture) while strategic differences around technology and critical minerals persist toward localization and tighter controls.

• **Incremental tariff progress**: Reciprocal tariff reductions on approximately US$30 billion of non-sensitive goods suggest both sides are willing to offer incremental stability, though the improvement in business confidence will be concentrated in non-sensitive sectors.

• **Policy measures deemed insufficient**: China faces persistent deflationary pressures and weak domestic demand as old growth drivers diminish; recent measures like mortgage subsidies and rate reductions are seen as inadequate to address the structural slowdown.

• **Consumption support accelerates tech**: Xing argues that helping Chinese consumers is not just a social priority but will sustain and accelerate the country's ongoing technological transformation ("Industrial Revolution 5.0"), countering the "fallacy of composition" that stimulating consumption undermines growth.

articles.title: Kurt Campbell on US deterrence, the Quad, Aukus and Taiwan after Xi-Trump summit
articles.summary:
- Kurt Campbell, known as the Biden administration's "Asia tsar," served as White House coordinator for Indo-Pacific affairs (2021–2024) and deputy secretary of state (2024–2025); he was a key architect of the Obama-era "pivot to Asia," helped develop the Quad, and shaped the "small yard, high fence" technology competition strategy.

- Campbell identifies a shift in US-China dynamics: both leaders are motivated to stabilize the relationship, driven by a mix of competitive self-interest and genuine cooperation desires.

- Campbell critiques President Trump's approach for prioritizing US-China relationship-building over allied partnerships, citing the deterioration with Canada—including Canada's reported interest in joining the EU—as "quite shocking" and troubling.

- His core argument is that America's enduring advantage is "allied scale," and that US technology strategy and global order efforts are best achieved through a strong posture with allies and partners alongside, not instead of, stabilizing the US-China relationship.

articles.title: TV showman Robert Chua spells out his vision for his vast collection of Chinese antiquities
articles.summary:
- **Robert Chua Wah-peng**, originally from Singapore, began collecting Chinese antiquities in 1967 upon arriving in Hong Kong and became serious about the hobby after his first visit to mainland China in 1979, routinely buying from dealers on Hollywood Road for decades.

- His collection, estimated at possibly **hundreds of thousands of pieces**, spans nearly every major Chinese dynasty — from Neolithic pottery to Qing ceramics — and includes blue-and-white porcelain, jade accessories, fossilised dinosaur eggs, wedding cabinets, horse sculptures, and Han-period terracotta figures.

- Chua is notably unconventional among collectors: he does not require gloves, does not store items behind glass, does not track a precise count of his holdings, and insists he buys solely for **beauty rather than investment value**, often purchasing multiples of items he loves to share with others.

- A standout theme in his collection is **mingqi** — ancient Chinese funerary "spirit objects" including miniature models of dwellings, animals, and figures — whose display in a living home is considered inauspicious in Chinese tradition, yet Chua keeps and engages with them openly.

articles.title: Hong Kong’s historic vessels sail into the future
articles.summary:
• The Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF) owns and maintains five historic wooden vessels, including Way Foong (built 1930 for HSBC by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company) and Java (a 1935-built government vessel known for its nearly 4.5cm-thick Burmese-teak deck planks and reputation as "almost unsinkable").

• HKHVF's CEO Philip Giannecchini states the organization aims to promote Hong Kong's maritime heritage and nurture future generations of boaters and ocean-lovers through the preservation of locally built vessels.

• The foundation grew out of an early-2000s chance discovery of Java in Tai Tam Harbour, which inspired a founding member to pursue broader historical acquisitions, ultimately leading to the organisation's formal founding.

• Historians have identified nine extant pre-1950s boats built in Hong Kong, with some now in the HKHVF collection, others privately owned, and at least one (Mon Lei) whose whereabouts remain unknown.

articles.title: Southeast Asia battles Big Tech to protect children online
articles.summary:
• Indonesia introduced some of Southeast Asia's strictest rules in March, barring under-16s from "high-risk" social media, but enforcement is undermined by children simply lying about their age, rendering restrictions largely ineffective without stronger age-verification systems from Big Tech.

• Platforms have responded with varying degrees of compliance: TikTok raised its minimum age to 16 and deactivated 9 million underage accounts by October; Meta and YouTube also raised minimum ages and began phased deactivations; Roblox now uses facial scanning to estimate users' ages in Indonesia.

• Indonesia has set a deadline of end-2025 for tech companies to complete comprehensive self-assessments on how their algorithms, age-verification, and ad-targeting systems protect children, backed by a sanctions mechanism allowing fines of up to 6% of global revenue—potentially around US$12 billion for Meta alone.

• Regional governments including Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Singapore are shifting from urging platforms to self-regulate toward imposing enforceable rules; Meta's recent US$18 billion settlement with US states over child addiction allegations highlights the growing legal and financial risks facing tech firms over child safety.

articles.title: Pacing problem: can AI fears overcome US-China race dynamics and force a slowdown?
articles.summary:
• **Leading US AI executives** – including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman, and Elon Musk – have called for "pacing" (slowing down) frontier AI development, citing fears that capabilities are outpacing safeguards; Amodei escalated the case by addressing the UN Security Council and warning of an existential threat.

• **Despite public calls for restraint**, these companies remain locked in an expensive domestic tech race and a costly US-China competition, making a near-term slowdown highly unlikely, analysts told the South China Morning Post.

• **China's AI progress persists despite US semiconductor export controls**: models from DeepSeek and Moonshot AI remain competitive with US counterparts in price and capability, challenging trillion-dollar valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic and undermining US claims of global AI leadership.

• **President Trump dismissed calls for an AI slowdown**, calling fears of AI destroying humanity "a hoax" on social media, raising doubts about whether pacing can gain traction without the support of one of the world's most powerful political leaders ahead of his summit with China's Xi Jinping.

articles.title: From fishing boats to Michelin stars: Vietnam’s CoCo Dining turns the humble into haute cuisine
articles.summary:
• Chef Vo Thanh Vuong, who grew up in Phan Thiet fishing full-time after his family's boat sank in 2000, is now a successful chef in Ho Chi Minh City with his restaurant CoCo Dining, bridging his fishing roots with fine dining.

• Vuong regularly returns to Vung Tau's coast to fish and source ingredients directly, demonstrating a deep, hands-on connection to the sea and its produce that informs his culinary approach.

• His cooking philosophy centers on ingredient quality over complexity: "When an ingredient is truly good, you don't need to do much to it," reflecting his fisherman's understanding of freshness and restraint.

• His kitchen style blends two modes — the fast, utilitarian cooking of a fisherman at sea and the deliberate, refined technique of a trained chef — using simple preparations like beer-steamed crabs, tamarind-pineapple hotpot, and lime-cured fish.

• Vuong's story illustrates a broader trend in Vietnam's food scene, where chefs from humble, coastal backgrounds are elevating local, traditional ingredients into haute cuisine and gaining international recognition.

articles.title: Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
articles.summary:
• **Tourism recovery lagging post-pandemic**: Thailand attracted nearly 40 million visitors in 2019 (a Southeast Asian record), but only 32.9 million arrived last year; the Tourism Authority of Thailand has lowered its 2026 forecast to 30–34 million, citing geopolitical conflicts driving up oil prices and international airfares.

• **Economic impact is significant**: Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of Thailand's economy, spanning luxury resorts, budget operators, and traditional attractions; a prolonged strong baht has also pushed budget-conscious travelers toward cheaper alternatives in Vietnam and Malaysia.

• **Shifting travel patterns hurt group-dependent businesses**: Post-COVID, mass tour groups have largely been replaced by "free, independent tourists" (FITs), devastating businesses like Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm, which once received 100–200 large tour buses per day but now sees only a handful.

• **Thailand's patience with misbehaving tourists is wearing thin**: Years of foreign tourist misconduct have eroded public goodwill, prompting the country to reconsider its open-door tourism policies, though specific examples and policy details are beyond the article's visible portion.

articles.title: Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
articles.summary:
• **COE and ownership costs are driving Singaporeans away from car ownership**: The Certificate of Entitlement (COE) for private cars has skyrocketed from S$10,000 in 2006 to over S$112,000 by 2024. Rising road tax, fuel, maintenance, insurance, and Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) fees further compound the financial burden of driving.

• **Private car numbers are declining**: Land Transport Authority figures for July 2024 show 516,237 privately owned cars, the lowest since 2019. However, rental, ride-hailing, and corporate cars have increased, and privately owned vehicles still make up 79% of all cars on the road.

• **ERP charges returned to Orchard Road**: For the first time since the pandemic began in 2020, congestion-charging fees were reinstated in Singapore's main shopping district at the start of August 2024.

• **Government pushes a "car-lite" strategy through infrastructure investment and campaigns**: The Land Transport Authority's "Move Lite" campaign, launched in 2022, promotes walking, cycling, and public transport use. The government is investing in public transport and active mobility infrastructure while managing vehicle ownership and road usage to optimize Singapore's limited land area.

articles.title: As the US weighs restrictions on cloud computing, how will China’s AI sector adapt?
articles.summary:
- Chinese AI developers have bypassed US chip export bans for years by using proxy entities to lease overseas data centre capacity in Southeast Asia, Japan, and the Middle East, training models on cutting-edge Nvidia processors outside US regulatory reach.

- The US Congress is now reportedly weighing legislation to restrict foreign remote access to cloud computing, and executive agencies are reviewing cloud-leasing loopholes, threatening to close what has been China's critical workaround around hardware bans.

- This impending crackdown could reshape the global AI ecosystem by challenging Southeast Asia's data centre boom, squeezing Nvidia's international revenues, and forcing Beijing to accelerate its domestic semiconductor development.

- Demand from Chinese developers has significantly boosted Nvidia's overseas sales, with global cloud rental rates surging—leading provider Nebius Group raised Nvidia chip rental prices by roughly 30% in June with a further 21% increase set for October 1, and hyperscaler rates for Nvidia's A100 processors climbing to US$3.75 per hour.

- Some Chinese engineering teams have employed creative workarounds to support cross-border training, including physically transporting hard drives containing 80 terabytes of data from Beijing to Malaysia to save months of transfer time, and using blockchain-based transactions to maintain secrecy.

commentary:
# 泰国旅游业的困境：全球资本流动中的从属经济体之痛

## 一、现象描述

泰国旅游业占GDP约五分之一，疫情后外国游客数从2019年近4000万回落至3290万，2026年预测再度下调，叠加游客失范行为引发的社会抵触。

## 二、政治经济学定位

泰国旅游业的萎缩绝非"游客素质"的表面问题，而是全球资本积累体系中从属经济体所固有的结构性脆弱性的集中暴露。旅游业本质上是一种特殊的服务商品生产与流通形式：泰国以低廉的劳动力价格和自然资源禀赋，向全球市场出售以"度假体验"为包装的服务商品。这一交换过程的核心，仍然是劳动力商品化条件下剩余价值的榨取——正如马克思所揭示的，"劳动力的买者消费劳动力，就是叫劳动力的卖者按摩师、服务员、导游劳动"。泰国数百万旅游服务业工人每日为跨国消费者提供"微笑服务"，其劳动所创造的价值远超资本支付给他们的劳动力价值，其中的差额——剩余价值——沿着全球旅游资本链向上流动，被航空公司、国际酒店集团、数字平台等环节所截取。

## 三、深层结构分析

泰国经济对旅游业的过度依赖，是冷战后全球劳动分工体系强加的"比较优势陷阱"的产物。国家资本将大量生产性资源——土地、基础设施、人力——投入非生产性的服务领域，而非用于构建独立完整的产业体系。文章中提到越南和马来西亚凭借"更便宜的替代"吸引预算型游客，恰恰说明这一领域的竞争已演变为劳动者工资水平的"竞次"（race to the bottom）：谁能更廉价地出售本国劳动力的使用价值，谁就能在争夺外国消费者购买力的战争中胜出。泰铢走强导致的客源流失，从本质上讲不过是汇率波动对利润率的冲击——当泰国劳动力以国际货币计价后变得"更贵"，资本便如马克思在分析地租和商业资本时所揭示的那样，自然流向回报更高的地域。

疫情后"大团队游"向"自由行"的转型，同样具有深层政治经济学含义。大型旅行社所组织的包价旅游，是一种相对集中的商品流通形式，其利润在供应链中的分配较为稳定；而自由行则使全球消费者通过数字平台直接对接泰国底层服务提供者，进一步瓦解了泰国本土中间资本的利润空间，将泰国更彻底地卷入全球资本的直接支配之下。

## 四、阶级与利益分析

谁受益？国际航空资本、跨国数字平台和全球连锁酒店集团，从泰国劳动力的廉价化中稳定获利。谁受损？泰国底层旅游服务业劳动者首当其冲——他们是文章中那个"开放的鳄鱼池"里被消费的主体，工资在汇率波动和客流不稳中剧烈摇摆。其次，泰国中小旅游资本（如鳄鱼农场经营者查伦家族）也沦为全球需求波动的附属物，自身毫无对经济结构的掌控权。

## 五、主流叙事批判

该文将矛盾的核心引向"游客行为失范"——酗酒、斗殴、破坏公物——将其框定为文化冲突与国民情感问题。这一叙事有意无意地遮蔽了真正的矛盾：泰国经济对全球资本流动的结构性依附。所谓"耐心耗尽"的话语，将劳工的结构性剥削转化为民族自尊的情绪议题，从而回避了追问：泰国的经济增长模式本身是否公正？当一个国家将五分之一的经济命脉系于外国消费者的随意选择之上时，其劳动者所承受的波动性风险由谁承担？

## 六、解放前景

出路在于打破对旅游业的结构性依赖。国家应当将资本积累的重心从服务商品的出口转向生产性部门的自主发展——建立独立的制造业体系、发展农业科技、投资基础设施的生产性使用。同时，旅游业内部的利润分配必须重塑：将旅游收入更多地导向劳动者工资和公共服务领域，而非任由剩余价值通过全球资本链外流。唯有如此，泰国的劳动者才能从全球旅游资本的"附属物"——正如马克思所言，"工人从机器的附属物变成了机器体系的附属物"——变为自身劳动成果的真正所有者。
